cards.text: Paul, an apostle of Jesus, is writing a letter to God's people in Rome. He just finished a long list of what people do when they turn away from God: greed, envy, gossip, arrogance, the whole lineup. Now he turns to the one who passes judgment on everybody on that list.

cards.question: Paul tells the person passing judgment on others that they have no excuse. What reason does he give?

cards.text: Caught pointing at somebody for the exact same thing. That's me in the junk drawer, telling the dead batteries I shared it with to quit lying around doing nothing. Friend. I was lying RIGHT NEXT to them.

cards.question: Paul says God's judgment against those who do such things is based on truth.

cards.text: Then Paul asks the judge: you condemn others and do the same things, and you think you'll escape God's judgment? Or are you ignoring the riches of His kindness, tolerance and patience?

cards.question: Paul says the judge doesn't realize where God's kindness leads. Where does it lead?

cards.text: But Paul says the judge has a hard and unrepentant heart. And a heart like that isn't just sitting there. It's piling something up for later.

cards.question: Paul says a hard and unrepentant heart is storing up ___ against itself for the day God's righteous judgment is revealed.

cards.text: Storing up wrath. That's like shoving every bill into the junk drawer without opening it. Friend, those bills are not going away. They're just WAITING for the day somebody opens that drawer.
Then Paul says God "will repay each one according to his deeds." Each one. Nobody gets skipped.

cards.question: Some people keep at doing good, seeking glory, honor and immortality. What does Paul say God will give them?
Paul says there will be peace for those who are self-seeking, reject the truth and follow wickedness.

cards.text: Paul keeps going: there will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek.

cards.question: For everyone who does good, Paul says glory, honor and peace come to the Jew but not to the Greek.
Evil brings trouble and good brings glory, for the Jew and for the Greek alike. What reason does Paul give?

answers.text: God gives the Jews more time

cards.text: No favoritism. No VIP line. No "but I know the owner." Trust me, friend, I tried "I know the owner" my first week in the junk drawer. I was saying it to a rubber band.
Now Paul brings in the law. He says all who sin apart from the law will also perish apart from the law.

cards.question: And Paul says all who sin under the law will be ___ by the law.

cards.text: Then Paul gets specific about who will be declared righteous before God. This one matters, friend. Lean in.

cards.question: Who does Paul say will be declared righteous before God?

cards.text: Hearing isn't doing. I can read a cookie recipe out loud fifty times, with FEELING. Still no cookies. Not one crumb. Not until I turn on the oven.
Then Paul talks about Gentiles, people who don't have the law. When they do by nature what the law requires, he says they are a law to themselves.

cards.question: When Gentiles do what the law requires without having the law, what does Paul say that shows?

answers.text: The law's work is written on their hearts
They secretly studied the law at home
They learned it from the people of Israel

cards.question: Paul says their ___ also bear witness, with their thoughts either accusing or defending them.
Paul points to the day when God will judge men's secrets. Through whom will God judge them?

cards.text: Paul says that's what his gospel proclaims. Friend, I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and I can tell you: there's no back of the drawer God can't see.

findings.problem: The card states facts from outside the passage but cites only Romans 2:1. These facts are that Paul is an apostle (Rom 1:1), that he writes to God's people in Rome (Rom 1:7), and the vice list of greed, envy, gossip and arrogance (Rom 1:29-30). None of them carries its reference.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The card says Paul turns to 'the one who passes judgment on everybody on that list.' Romans 2:1 says only 'you who pass judgment on another' and doesn't say the judge is judging the people in the chapter 1 list. The card closes a connection the text leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: This story card is only a joke. It adds no part of the passage and only reacts to Romans 2:1, which cards 1 and 2 already covered.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: The joke invents a new drawer moment: Papa Dorin telling the dead batteries to quit lying around. It also sits uneasily with the backstory, where in the drawer 'He didn't talk much. He didn't joke at all.' Made-up moments are allowed only around his bakery.

rule.text: He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.
Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card says 'you condemn others.' Romans 2:3 says 'pass judgment on others.'

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.
Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Cards 7 and 8 make the heart the one storing up wrath 'against itself.' In Romans 2:5, the person stores up wrath against himself because of his hard and unrepentant heart. The heart is the cause, not the one doing the storing.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: This story card is only a joke and a recap ('Storing up wrath.'). It adds no part of the passage beyond card 8.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.
Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

The joke invents a new backstory moment: trying 'I know the owner' on a rubber band during his first week in the drawer. The backstory says that in that period 'He didn't talk much. He didn't joke at all.'

rule.text: He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: The card has 3 sentences. It also carries no moment of the passage, only a teaser ('This one matters, friend. Lean in.'). That leaves no context to reason from before card 4.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card is a recap ('Hearing isn't doing.') plus a joke. It adds no part of the passage beyond card 4.

findings.problem: The right answer ('The law's work is written on their hearts') sounds like Scripture. The wrong answers sound modern and casual ('They secretly studied the law at home'), so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
